items.title: Explaining decisions made with AI, Part 3: Organisational roles and functions for explaining AI
items.publisher: Information Commissioner's Office and The Alan Turing Institute
items.locator: Section 'What if we use an AI system supplied by a third party?'
items.why: Source of the quotation: the buyer, as controller, answers for whether a bought system can produce an explanation. Good-practice guidance, not a statutory code; under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025.
items.quote: the primary responsibility for ensuring that the AI system you use is capable of producing an appropriate explanation for the decision recipient

items.title: Explaining decisions made with AI, Part 2, Task 3: Build your system to ensure you are able to extract relevant information
items.publisher: Information Commissioner's Office and The Alan Turing Institute
items.locator: Sections 'Select an appropriately explainable model' and 'What types of models are we choosing between?'
items.why: Source of the figure (11 techniques largely interpretable, four broadly 'black box'). Says model selection matters whether procuring or building, and that the choice of an opaque model should be documented. Under review.
items.quote: Selecting an appropriate model is important whether you are procuring a model from an external vendor, or looking to build a bespoke system in-house.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 25: Data protection by design and by default
items.why: Measures must be in place 'both at the time of the determination of the means for processing and at the time of the processing itself'. Does not mention explainability by name. Amended 5 February 2026 (paragraphs 1A, 1B, 4, 5 on children); no outstanding effects shown.
items.quote: both at the time of the determination of the means for processing and at the time of the processing itself

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 22C: Safeguards for automated decision-making
items.why: The four safeguards a controller must provide for significant decisions taken solely by automated means 'by or on behalf of' it. In force 5 February 2026 (S.I. 2026/82). Says nothing about suppliers or access to a model's reasoning.
items.quote: enable the data subject to obtain human intervention on the part of the controller in relation to such decisions

items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: What are the accountability and governance implications of AI?
items.why: Requirements to be specified at the procurement stage; if a third-party system cannot be assessed, opt for a different one as good practice; review outsourced services regularly. Under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025.
items.quote: You are also required to specify your requirements at the procurement stage, rather than addressing trade-offs afterwards.

items.title: Guidelines for AI procurement
items.locator: Top 10 considerations, no. 8 'Avoid Black Box algorithms and vendor lock in'; section on drafting the invitation to tender
items.why: Explainability as a design criterion and a tender requirement; process logs for auditability. Written for public-sector buyers; published 8 June 2020 and not updated since.
items.quote: Encourage explainability and interpretability of algorithms and make this one of your design criteria.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 13: Transparency and provision of information to deployers
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.locator: Art. 13(1); see also 13(2)-(3) on instructions for use
items.quote: their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret a system's output and use it appropriately
items.why: The binding EU design-stage rule: a high-risk system must be built so the organisation deploying it can interpret its output, and must come with instructions for use. The Commission's copy of the consolidated text (stated as at 27 July 2026), not the Official Journal. EU law: it matters to UK firms only so far as the Act applies to them; no application date is given here.

items.title: Data protection audit framework, Artificial intelligence toolkit: Contracts and third parties
items.locator: Control measure 'Before procuring AI systems, datasets or coding, there has been appropriate due diligence...', list 'Ways to meet our expectations'
items.quote: Choose AI models that offer transparency and explainability.
items.why: What the regulator's auditors look for before a purchase: due diligence, explainable models chosen, and performance terms written into supplier contracts. Carries the 'under review' banner following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; the page shows no publication date, so the year is the year read. Data protection only.

items.title: SS1/23 Model risk management principles for banks
items.publisher: Bank of England, Prudential Regulation Authority
items.locator: Principle 3.5 'Model development documentation', point (a), PDF p.24; see also Principle 2.6 on vendor models
items.quote: Firms should ensure the level of detail in the documentation of third-party vendor models is sufficient to validate the firm's use of the model.
items.why: A supervisory expectation that documentation for a bought-in model must be good enough for the buyer to validate its own use, and kept up to date. Sector-specific: addressed to banks, building societies and PRA-designated investment firms with internal model approval; covers all models, not only AI.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in UK financial services - 2024
items.publisher: Bank of England and Financial Conduct Authority
items.locator: Executive summary, 'Understanding of AI systems' and 'Third-party exposure'
items.quote: This is largely due to the use of third-party models where respondent firms noted a lack of complete understanding compared to models developed internally.
items.why: Regulators' survey evidence that bought-in models are where firms' understanding is weakest: 46% reported only partial understanding of the AI they use, and a third of use cases were third-party implementations. Financial services only; a survey of regulated firms, self-reported.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government
items.locator: Section 'Transparency and explainability' (under using AI safely and responsibly)
items.quote: Transparency can be limited by proprietary and 'black box' commercial tools
items.why: Government's own guidance says explainability depends on the technology chosen and must be considered at design, and names proprietary commercial tools as the usual limit. Written for civil servants and public bodies; guidance, not a binding rule for companies.

items.title: Commentary: Model Contractual Clauses for the public procurement of AI (MCC-AI)
items.publisher: European Commission, Public Buyers Community (Community of Practice on Public Procurement of AI)
items.locator: Section 1 (Background), PDF p.3; Article 14 commentary, PDF pp.11-12
items.quote: an obligation on the Supplier to cooperate in explaining, at an individual level, how the AI system reached such an outcome or decision
items.why: A worked example of a contractual explainability obligation: model clauses that bind the supplier to help explain individual decisions (clause 14, aligned with Article 86 of the EU AI Act). Voluntary templates drafted for EU public bodies, not UK law and not written for private buyers; the PDF carries no dateline (the year is from the publisher's file path and its resource page).

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Section 3.5 'Explainable and Interpretable', p.16 (PDF p.21); Table 3, MEASURE 2.9; Table 1, GOVERN 6
items.quote: Risk from lack of explainability may be managed by describing how AI systems function
items.why: A widely cited US risk framework treats explainability as a characteristic to be designed, measured and documented, and third-party systems as a governed risk. Voluntary and from the United States; it sets no procurement or contract terms.

items.title: Model Artificial Intelligence Governance Framework, Second Edition
items.publisher: Info-communications Media Development Authority and Personal Data Protection Commission, Singapore
items.locator: Section 3 'Operations management', 'Explainability', paras 3.26 onwards, PDF p.45
items.quote: the organisation can consider requesting assistance from the AI solution provider as they may be better placed to explain how the solution functions
items.why: International comparator: Singapore's model framework also places explanation on the deploying organisation and points it back to the supplier where the system was bought. Voluntary, non-UK, and softer than the UK regulator's position ("can consider").

items.title: Stop Explaining Black Box Machine Learning Models for High Stakes Decisions and Use Interpretable Models Instead
items.publisher: Cynthia Rudin (arXiv; published in Nature Machine Intelligence, 2019)
items.quote: There is a way forward -- it is to design models that are inherently interpretable.
items.why: The best-known research argument for settling explainability when the model is chosen: explaining an opaque model afterwards, the author says, is likely to perpetuate bad practice. Author's pre-publication version (v3, 22 September 2019) of a 2019 Nature Machine Intelligence article; a position paper, not an empirical study.

items.title: Model Cards for Model Reporting
items.publisher: Margaret Mitchell and others (arXiv; published in Proceedings of FAT* 2019)
items.quote: we recommend that released models be accompanied by documentation detailing their performance characteristics
items.why: The origin of the standard supplier document a buyer can ask for: intended use, evaluation across groups and limits. Authors' repository copy of a conference paper (FAT* 2019); a proposal with two worked examples, not evidence of effect.

items.title: The 2024 Foundation Model Transparency Index
items.publisher: Rishi Bommasani and others, Stanford Center for Research on Foundation Models (arXiv)
items.quote: We find that developers now score 58 out of 100 on average, a 21 point improvement over FMTI 2023.
items.why: Evidence on how much the large model suppliers disclose: 14 developers scored against 100 indicators averaged 58, up from 37. Shows why documentation has to be asked for, and that asking produces it. Preprint (v2, 4 March 2025); scores rest partly on developers' own reports; covers general-purpose model developers, not every AI vendor.
